newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU investment bank to play key role in EMU deal.
newsitem.headline: EU investment bank to play key role in EMU deal.

text.p: The European Investment Bank, one of the world's largest development agencies, has emerged as a key player in an EU compromise plan that meets France's demands for greater action on jobs growth.

In talks between EU finance ministers on Sunday night, diplomats said several proposals were put forward in an initial draft that would be part of a political resolution to help the 18 million unemployed in the 15-nation bloc.

Importantly, the one aspect that focused on specific funding for new employment programmes includes the EIB, a profit-making institution outside the EU's budget and involved in the financing of large infrastructure projects.
"The EIB has made serious profits," said one EU diplomat. "The question is whether you can finance certain projects with their money."
Speaking to reporters after the Sunday dinner, Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told reporters that extending the scope of the bank's activities was an area the ministers were considering.
He stressed, however, that any involvement of the EIB would have to be based on "sound lending."

The inclusion of the EIB in a jobs resolution would give the document added bite and hopefully allow France to sign off on the stability and growth pact, a measure designed to keep public finances under control among countries inside monetary union.
France last week stunned its European partners when it asked for more time to study the pact, agreed in principle by EU leaders last December in Dublin after lengthy negotiations.

With the new French government elected on a platform of greater jobs growth, French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin is under pressure to return from the EU summit with more than just a set of neatly crafted phrases on employment growth.
In addition to EIB lending, diplomats said there would be an effort to speed the legislative adoption of an employment chapter to the Maastricht Treaty.
The amendment would focus on greater cooperation between EU governments to promote jobs, but avoid any reference to new money for large-scale programmes.
"I don't expect funds will be released (for job creation schemes), but there might be some recourse to the European bank," Greek Deputy Foreign Minister George Papandreou told a news conference.

Germany and several other states have remained strongly opposed the use of surplus funds in the EU budget for new jobs schemes, believing that the responsibility for employment growth rests primarily with national governments.

Moreover, in a period when virtually all under pressure to tighten their fiscal belts ahead of monetary union, any extra money in the EU budget should be returned to national governments to alleviate the stress of curbing expenditure.
